summary: This chapter sorts life insurance products into families so you can tell them apart on the exam. Questions usually describe a buyer's need or a policy feature and ask which product fits, so focus on how premiums, cash value, and the death benefit behave in each one.

Whole life is permanent coverage with a fixed premium, a guaranteed cash value that grows each year, and a death benefit that does not change. Paying the premiums over a shorter time, as in limited-pay or single-premium life, does not shorten the coverage; it only makes each payment larger and builds cash value faster. Universal life separates the protection from a cash account, so the owner can change premiums and, within limits, the death benefit. Variable products invest the cash value in separate accounts, so values can rise or fall, while indexed life credits interest linked to a market index with a floor that protects against loss.

Term insurance covers only a set period and usually has no cash value, which makes it the cheapest way to buy a large amount of protection. Level, decreasing, annually renewable, and return-of-premium term differ in how the face amount and premium change. Annuities work the other way around from life insurance: instead of protecting against dying too soon, they protect against outliving your money by turning a sum into a stream of payments.

concepts.definition: The savings part of a permanent policy that builds up over time. The owner can borrow against it or receive it by surrendering the policy.
concepts.tip: Term has no cash value; permanent policies do.

concepts.definition: Flexible permanent insurance where premiums go into a cash account, monthly insurance charges come out, and the account earns interest.
concepts.tip: Flexible premium, flexible death benefit.

concepts.definition: Permanent insurance whose cash value is invested in separate accounts chosen by the owner, so the value is not guaranteed.
concepts.tip: Variable = investment risk on the owner, and a securities license for the agent.

concepts.definition: Term coverage that renews each year without new proof of health, with a premium that goes up every year as the insured ages.
concepts.tip: Cheap at first, rises every year.

concepts.definition: An immediate annuity is bought with one payment and starts paying within about a year. A deferred annuity grows for a period before payments begin.
concepts.tip: Immediate = single premium, payout soon.

concepts.definition: An annuity payout that gives the highest income per payment but stops at the annuitant's death, with nothing left for heirs.
concepts.tip: Highest payment, no refund.

points: Matching a need to a product, such as a shrinking loan to decreasing term, is a common question style.
Know which products put the investment risk on the owner: variable whole life, variable universal life, and variable annuities.
Annuity questions often ask which payout option gives the largest check or which one guarantees a refund.

summary: This chapter covers the promises written into a life policy and the extras a buyer can add. Many questions give a short story, such as a missed premium or a wrong age on the application, and ask which provision decides the outcome.

Standard provisions protect both sides. The entire contract clause says the policy plus the attached application is the whole agreement. The free look period lets a new owner return the policy for a full refund. The grace period keeps coverage alive for a short time after a missed premium, and reinstatement lets an owner bring a lapsed policy back, usually within a few years, with proof of insurability and back premiums. The suicide clause limits the payout to a refund of premiums if the insured dies by suicide in the first one or two years.

When an owner stops paying a cash value policy, the nonforfeiture options keep the value from being lost. Dividends from a participating policy can be taken in cash, used to lower the premium, left to earn interest, or used to buy paid-up additions. Settlement options decide how the beneficiary receives the death benefit, such as a lump sum, interest only, a fixed period, a fixed amount, or a life income.

concepts.definition: A rider that pays an extra amount, often equal to the face amount, if the insured dies from an accident within a set time after the injury.
concepts.tip: Often called double indemnity.

concepts.definition: Used on a child's policy; it waives future premiums if the adult who pays them dies or becomes disabled.
concepts.tip: Protects the payor, not the insured child.

concepts.definition: An option that pays an overdue premium with a loan from the policy's cash value so the policy does not lapse.
concepts.tip: Needs enough cash value to work.

concepts.definition: If the insured and the primary beneficiary die in the same accident and it is unclear who died first, the insured is treated as living longer, so the money goes to the contingent beneficiary.
concepts.tip: Keeps the money from passing through the beneficiary's estate.

concepts.definition: The ways a death benefit can be paid out: lump sum, interest only, fixed period, fixed amount, or life income.
concepts.tip: Fixed period sets the time; fixed amount sets the check size.

concepts.definition: A loan from the insurer using the cash value as security. Any unpaid loan and interest is subtracted from the death benefit.
concepts.tip: No credit check, but it lowers the payout if not repaid.

points: Story questions about a death during the grace period or after a wrong age is found are common.
Know the difference between reduced paid-up and extended term, since both keep coverage without new premiums.
Beneficiary questions test revocable versus irrevocable designations and what happens with a minor beneficiary.

summary: This chapter follows a life policy from the first meeting to the day it is delivered. Questions test what the agent must do on the application, what the insurer may look at during underwriting, and when coverage actually begins.

The application gathers facts about the proposed insured and the owner. Changes must be initialed by the applicant, and an incomplete application is sent back rather than guessed at. When a new policy will replace an existing one, the agent must follow the state replacement rules. Federal rules also apply at the point of sale, such as privacy notices under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and, for cash value products, an anti-money-laundering program with reporting of suspicious activity.

During underwriting the insurer decides whether to accept the risk and at what price, using the application, medical exams, attending physician statements, the MIB, and consumer reports. Stranger-originated life insurance, where outside investors arrange a policy on someone they have no insurable interest in, is prohibited in most states. At delivery, the agent explains the policy, any riders, exclusions, and ratings, and collects any unpaid premium.

concepts.definition: A real financial or emotional stake in the insured's life, such as a spouse, a close relative, a business partner, or a creditor up to the debt.
concepts.tip: You may always insure your own life.

concepts.definition: A representation is a statement believed to be true; only a material false one can void the contract. A warranty is a guarantee that a statement is exactly true.
concepts.tip: Applications use representations.

concepts.definition: An applicant with higher-than-normal risk who is accepted at a higher premium, a lower benefit, or with an exclusion.
concepts.tip: Rated, not declined.

concepts.definition: A contract where the two sides may exchange very unequal values, because the payout depends on an uncertain event.
concepts.tip: A small premium can buy a large death benefit.

concepts.definition: A contract written by one party and accepted as is by the other, so any unclear wording is read in favor of the insured.
concepts.tip: Insurer wrote it, insurer loses ties.

concepts.definition: A signed statement the agent collects at delivery when no premium was paid with the application, confirming the insured's health has not changed.
concepts.tip: No money up front means a health statement at delivery.

points: Questions ask who must sign the application and how to correct a wrong answer on it.
Know when insurable interest is required and that it is not needed at the time of death.
Expect at least one question naming the four legal features of an insurance contract.

summary: This chapter connects life insurance to bigger financial goals: retirement, business needs, family needs, and taxes. Questions are often short scenarios that ask which plan or tax rule applies.

Needs analysis looks at what a family would need if the earner died, such as final expenses, debts, income for survivors, and education. Businesses use life insurance to protect against the loss of a key person and to fund buy-sell agreements, so the surviving owners have cash to buy a deceased owner's share. Group life insurance is usually term coverage under a master contract, and the employer may pay all the premium (noncontributory) or share the cost with employees (contributory).

Retirement plans are either qualified, meeting federal rules and getting tax benefits, or nonqualified, which can favor selected employees but give up some of those benefits. A life settlement is the sale of an existing policy by its owner to a third party for more than the cash surrender value but less than the death benefit. Social Security pays survivor benefits to eligible family members, which a needs analysis takes into account.

concepts.definition: A contract among business owners to buy a deceased or disabled owner's share at an agreed price, often funded with life insurance.
concepts.tip: Cross-purchase: owners insure each other; entity: the business insures each owner.

concepts.definition: The sale of an existing life policy by the owner to a third party who pays cash now, takes over the premiums, and collects the death benefit later.
concepts.tip: Owner sells the policy; different from STOLI, which starts without insurable interest.

concepts.definition: In a contributory plan employees pay part of the premium; in a noncontributory plan the employer pays all of it, and all eligible employees are usually covered.
concepts.tip: Noncontributory = employer pays 100%.

concepts.definition: A life policy that fails the federal 7-pay test because it was paid in too quickly. It stays in force, but loans and withdrawals lose the usual tax advantages of life insurance.
concepts.tip: Too much money too fast.

concepts.definition: A policy where the owner is not the insured, such as a parent owning a policy on a child or a business owning a policy on an employee.
concepts.tip: Owner controls the policy; insured is the measuring life.

points: Tax questions ask whether premiums are deductible and whether proceeds or dividends are taxable.
Know who owns, pays for, and receives the money in key person and buy-sell arrangements.
Group life questions test the conversion right when employment ends.

summary: This chapter is the largest part of the health half. It covers what each kind of health policy pays for and who it is designed for, so questions usually ask which policy fits a situation.

Disability income insurance pays a monthly benefit when illness or injury keeps the insured from working. Businesses can also buy coverage that pays the office's bills while an owner is disabled, coverage that funds a buyout of a disabled owner, and coverage on a key employee. Medical expense insurance ranges from basic hospital, surgical, and medical plans with first-dollar benefits to major medical plans with deductibles, coinsurance, and an out-of-pocket maximum. Managed care plans such as HMOs, PPOs, and POS plans control cost by using networks of providers.

Other policies fill gaps. Medicare supplement policies help pay costs that Medicare leaves to the patient, using standardized plans. Long-term care insurance pays for help with daily living at home, in assisted living, or in a nursing home. Group coverage is issued under a master contract to an employer, and continuation rules can let workers keep it for a time after they leave. Limited policies such as dental, vision, cancer, critical illness, hospital indemnity, and accident-only pay only for the risk they name, and short-term medical gives temporary coverage for a gap between plans.

concepts.definition: Basic plans pay set amounts for hospital, surgical, and doctor services, often with no deductible. Major medical covers a broad range of costs with a deductible, coinsurance, and a yearly out-of-pocket maximum.
concepts.tip: Basic = first-dollar, limited. Major medical = broad, cost sharing.

concepts.definition: A managed care plan that combines HMO and PPO features: a primary care doctor manages care, but members may go out of network at a higher cost.
concepts.tip: Decide at the point of service.

concepts.definition: An employer plan where workers set aside pretax pay for medical costs; unused money is generally lost at the end of the plan year, apart from limited carryover or grace period rules.
concepts.tip: Use it or lose it.

concepts.definition: An account funded only by the employer that pays back employees for qualified medical expenses.
concepts.tip: Employer money only.

concepts.definition: A policy that pays a fixed cash amount for each day the insured is in the hospital, no matter what the actual bills are.
concepts.tip: Pays a set amount per day.

concepts.definition: Skilled care is daily nursing ordered by a doctor; intermediate care is occasional nursing; custodial care is help with daily activities such as bathing and dressing.
concepts.tip: Custodial care is the most common and the least medical.

points: Expect questions that ask which disability product pays business expenses versus which one funds a buyout.
HMO, PPO, and POS questions test gatekeepers, referrals, and out-of-network coverage.
Know which account needs a high deductible plan and which one only the employer funds.

summary: This chapter covers the rules written into individual health policies. Most states base them on a model law with twelve mandatory provisions and eleven optional ones, so the exam often asks for a time limit or which provision applies.

The mandatory provisions set out the claim process and protect the insured: the entire contract, the time limit on certain defenses, the grace period, reinstatement, notice of claim, claim forms, proof of loss, time of payment of claims, payment of claims, physical examination and autopsy, legal actions, and change of beneficiary. Optional provisions let the insurer adjust benefits for things such as a change to a more hazardous occupation, a misstated age, or an illegal occupation.

Other clauses decide what the policy pays. A probationary period delays coverage for illness after the policy starts, while an elimination period is the waiting time before disability benefits begin. Deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments share costs with the insured. Renewability terms, from cancelable to noncancelable, decide whether the insurer can end the policy or raise its premium.

concepts.definition: If a lapsed policy is reinstated, accidents are covered right away, but sickness is covered only if it begins more than 10 days after reinstatement.
concepts.tip: Accident now, sickness after 10 days.

concepts.definition: The insurer must pay benefits promptly after receiving proof of loss; ongoing disability benefits are paid at least monthly.
concepts.tip: Prompt payment, monthly for disability.

concepts.definition: An optional provision that lets the insurer lower benefits if the insured moves to a more hazardous job, or lower the premium if the new job is safer.
concepts.tip: Riskier job, smaller benefit.

concepts.definition: The number of days a disability must last before benefits start. A longer elimination period means a lower premium.
concepts.tip: It works like a deductible measured in time.

concepts.definition: The way covered costs are shared after the deductible, such as 80% paid by the insurer and 20% by the insured, often up to a yearly limit.
concepts.tip: Deductible first, then the percentage split.

concepts.definition: The insurer must renew the policy to a stated age as long as premiums are paid, but it may raise rates for an entire class of insureds.
concepts.tip: Renewal guaranteed, price not.

points: Number questions about notice of claim, claim forms, proof of loss, and legal actions are very common.
Know the order of cost sharing: deductible, then coinsurance, up to the out-of-pocket limit.
Renewability questions ask who can cancel the policy and who can raise the premium.

summary: This chapter covers health and income programs run by the government and how private insurance works around them. Questions usually ask which program or which part of Medicare pays for a service.

Medicare is the federal health insurance program, mainly for older people. Part A pays for inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facility care after a qualifying hospital stay, hospice, and some home health care, and most people do not pay a premium for it because they paid Medicare taxes while working. Part B pays for doctor visits, outpatient care, and medical equipment and has a monthly premium. Part C lets people get their benefits through private Medicare Advantage plans, and Part D adds prescription drug coverage through private plans.

Medicaid pays health costs for people with low income and few assets and can pay for long-term nursing home care when a person qualifies financially. Social Security pays retirement, disability, and survivor benefits based on a worker's earnings record. Its disability definition is strict: the worker must be unable to do any substantial work, not just their own job.

concepts.definition: Hospital insurance that covers inpatient hospital stays, skilled nursing facility care after a qualifying hospital stay, hospice, and some home health care.
concepts.tip: A = admitted to the hospital.

concepts.definition: Medical insurance for doctor services, outpatient care, preventive services, and durable medical equipment, paid partly by a monthly premium.
concepts.tip: B = doctor bills.

concepts.definition: Private plans approved by Medicare that provide Part A and Part B benefits, often through HMO or PPO networks.
concepts.tip: C = combined, through a private company.

concepts.definition: A needs-based health program paid for by the federal and state governments and run by each state.
concepts.tip: Medicaid = aid for low income.

concepts.definition: Monthly income for insured workers who cannot do substantial gainful work because of a long-lasting or terminal condition.
concepts.tip: Strict definition: any work, not just your job.

points: Matching a service to Part A, B, C, or D is the most common question style.
Know that Medicare does not cover custodial long-term care, while Medicaid may for people who qualify.
Social Security disability questions test the strict definition and the waiting period.

summary: This chapter collects health insurance ideas that do not fit one policy type. Questions are short and usually test one definition or one tax rule.

Disability can be total, partial, residual, or recurrent. Total disability is defined by the policy, either as being unable to do your own occupation or any reasonable occupation. A recurrent disability provision treats a return of the same condition within a set time as the same disability, so a new elimination period does not start. Occupational coverage pays for injuries both on and off the job, while nonoccupational coverage pays only for those off the job, leaving work injuries to workers compensation.

When a person has more than one plan, coordination of benefits decides which plan pays first so the total paid does not go above the actual cost. Managed care controls cost through networks, referrals, and reviews of care. Workers compensation is required in almost every state and pays medical bills and lost wages for job injuries without anyone having to prove fault. Tax rules depend on who paid the premium.

concepts.definition: A provision that treats a relapse of the same condition within a stated period, often 6 months, as a continuation of the earlier disability, so no new elimination period applies.
concepts.tip: Same cause, short gap, same claim.

concepts.definition: Coverage that pays only for illness or injury that does not happen at work, because job-related losses are covered by workers compensation.
concepts.tip: Group disability is often nonoccupational.

concepts.definition: A program required in almost every state, paid for by employers, that covers medical care, lost wages, and rehabilitation for job-related injury or illness regardless of fault.
concepts.tip: No-fault, employer-paid.

concepts.definition: Benefits paid by health insurance to cover medical bills are generally not taxable income to the person receiving them.
concepts.tip: Reimbursed medical bills are not income.

concepts.definition: Health plans that offer dependent coverage must allow children to stay on a parent's plan until age 26 under federal law, and newborns are covered from birth when the plan covers dependents.
concepts.tip: Age 26 rule.

points: Disability definition questions compare own occupation, any occupation, residual, and recurrent.
Tax questions hinge on who paid the premium and whether it was paid with pretax or after-tax money.
Know which plan pays first when a person has two group plans.

summary: This chapter covers the agent's job as the first underwriter in the field. Questions test what the agent must explain, collect, and give to the applicant, and what happens when something on the application is wrong.

The agent asks every question on the application exactly as written and records the answers honestly, since the insurer relies on them to decide on the risk. The agent also explains how the insurer may gather information, such as medical records, the MIB, and consumer reports, gives the insurer's privacy notice, and tells the applicant when an investigative consumer report will be ordered under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. If the applicant pays the first premium, the agent gives a receipt, and the type of receipt decides when coverage can begin.

After the policy is issued, the agent delivers it, explains its provisions, riders, exclusions, and any rating, and makes sure the applicant understands what was bought. When a new policy replaces another one, the agent must follow the replacement rules so the client does not lose benefits without knowing it. The same contract law terms used for life insurance apply here too.

concepts.definition: The agent's work before the application reaches the insurer: screening the applicant, asking every question, collecting the first premium, and noting anything the underwriter should know.
concepts.tip: The agent is the first screen for risk.

concepts.definition: A federal law that protects the privacy of personal health information and limits how insurers and providers may use and share it.
concepts.tip: Protects health information.

concepts.definition: A federal law that sets rules for consumer reports, including telling applicants when a report is used and giving them a way to correct wrong information.
concepts.tip: Consumer reports must be fair and correctable.

concepts.definition: A receipt given when the first premium is paid with the application; coverage starts as of the application or exam date if the applicant qualifies as applied for.
concepts.tip: Coverage depends on being insurable.

concepts.definition: Buying a new policy that will cause an existing policy to be dropped, lapsed, or reduced. State rules require notices and comparisons so the client can decide fairly.
concepts.tip: Make sure the switch helps the client.

points: Questions ask what the agent should do when the premium was not collected with the application.
Know how to correct an error on the application and who must initial it.
Expect a question on what the MIB is and how insurers may use it.
